content: Then Jonah prayed to the LORD, his God, out of the fish’s belly. {{v:2}} He said, “I called because of my affliction to the LORD. He answered me. Out of the belly of Sheol I cried. You heard my voice. {{v:3}} For you threw me into the depths, in the heart of the seas. The flood was all around me. All your waves and your billows passed over me. {{v:4}} I said, ‘I have been banished from your sight; yet I will look again toward your holy temple.’ {{v:5}} The waters surrounded me, even to the soul. The deep was around me. The weeds were wrapped around my head. {{v:6}} I went down to the bottoms of the mountains. The earth barred me in forever; yet you have brought my life up from the pit, LORD my God. {{v:7}} “When my soul fainted within me, I remembered the LORD. My prayer came in to you, into your holy temple. {{v:8}} Those who regard vain idols forsake their own mercy. {{v:9}} But I will sacrifice to you with the voice of thanksgiving. I will pay that which I have vowed. Salvation belongs to the LORD.” {{v:10}} Then the LORD spoke to the fish, and it vomited out Jonah on the dry land.

facets.text: Jonah's prayer arises from within the fish's belly, the very place of his near-death and confinement, teaching that no depth or darkness places a soul beyond the reach of God's ear. The prophet cries 'out of the belly of Sheol' and is answered, revealing that repentant prayer can ascend to God even from the abyss. This grounds the Catholic conviction that God hears the contrite from every affliction, however self-inflicted.
facets.question: Can God hear a person's prayer even from the depths of despair or death?

facets.text: Jonah confesses that God himself 'threw me into the depths,' recognizing the storm and sea as the just consequence of his flight from the LORD's command. Yet the same divine hand that cast him down is the hand that 'brought my life up from the pit,' so that chastisement and mercy are seen as one continuous saving action. The passage teaches that God's discipline is not abandonment but a means of drawing the sinner back.
facets.question: Why does God allow suffering as a consequence of sin, and how is it part of his mercy?

facets.text: Even while banished from God's sight, Jonah resolves, 'yet I will look again toward your holy temple,' and declares that his prayer reached God 'into your holy temple.' The temple orientation reveals prayer as covenantal and directed toward the place of God's presence and sacrifice, foreshadowing the Christian's turning toward Christ, the true Temple and locus of atonement. Hope persists precisely by fixing the eyes on the sanctuary of divine mercy.
facets.question: What is the significance of turning toward the temple when praying in distress?

facets.text: Jonah's three days in the fish and his deliverance to dry land are read by the tradition, following Christ himself, as a sign of the Lord's death and resurrection. The prophet's descent into the watery pit and his being 'brought up' prefigure the Paschal Mystery, where Christ enters the depths of death and rises on the third day. This typology gives Jonah's ordeal a Christological depth beyond its literal event.
facets.question: How does Jonah in the fish prefigure the death and resurrection of Christ?

facets.text: Jonah contrasts those 'who regard vain idols' and thereby 'forsake their own mercy' with his own vow to 'sacrifice with the voice of thanksgiving.' Idolatry is presented as a self-inflicted loss of the very mercy God freely offers, while true worship responds to deliverance with grateful sacrifice and the fulfillment of vows. This anticipates the Eucharistic pattern of thanksgiving offered in return for salvation.
facets.question: How does clinging to idols cause a person to lose the mercy God offers?

facets.text: The prayer culminates in the confession, 'Salvation belongs to the LORD,' summarizing the whole psalm's movement from helplessness to rescue. Jonah, unable to save himself from the deep, learns that deliverance is entirely God's gift and not a human achievement. This declaration expresses the heart of biblical soteriology: salvation originates in God alone and is received in gratitude.
facets.question: What does it mean to confess that salvation belongs to God alone?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: Jonah's psalm of thanksgiving from within the fish moves from the depths of near-death to deliverance, teaching that God hears the afflicted, disciplines in mercy, and alone gives salvation; the tradition reads the ordeal as a sign of Christ's death and resurrection.

[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: God hears the contrite prayer even from Sheol and the abyss; no depth places a repentant soul beyond his reach.
[DOCTRINAL | inferential]: The God who cast Jonah into the depths as just consequence of his flight is the same God who raises him; chastisement is a form of mercy drawing the sinner back.
[SCRIPTURAL | traditional]: Turning toward God's holy temple expresses covenantal prayer directed to the place of presence and sacrifice, prefiguring Christ as the true Temple and locus of atonement.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: Jonah's descent into the pit and deliverance to dry land, per Christ's own words, prefigure the Paschal Mystery of death and third-day resurrection.
[MORAL | explicit]: Regarding vain idols forsakes one's own mercy, whereas grateful sacrifice and fulfilled vows are the fitting response to deliverance, anticipating Eucharistic thanksgiving.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: The confession 'Salvation belongs to the LORD' declares that rescue is wholly God's gift, received in gratitude and not achieved by human effort.
